Bridge is a card game for four players in two partnerships. You sit South and play with North, your bot partner, against West and East.\n\nEvery board has two parts: first the auction (bidding), then the play of 13 tricks.

In the auction each side says how many tricks it can win and with which trump suit. The highest bid becomes the contract, and that side must then win that many tricks.\n\nA bid of 3♥ means: “we will win 9 tricks (6 + 3) with hearts as trump.” A trick is four cards, one from each player, and the highest card wins it.

Every Ace is worth 4 points, King 3, Queen 2 and Jack 1. All 52 cards add up to 40, so an average hand has 10.\n\nWith about 12 points you can open the bidding. With fewer, say Pass. You and your partner together need about 25 points to make a game.

On your turn tap a call in the bidding box: a level from 1 to 7 with a suit or NT (no trump), or Pass. Each bid must be higher than the last one: first by level, then by suit, in the order shown above.

X (double) and XX (redouble) raise the stakes. The auction ends when three players pass in a row.

Not sure what a bid means? Tap any call in the auction list and the app explains it.

The player to the left of the declarer (the one who first named the contract’s suit for their side) leads the first card. Then the declarer’s partner lays their hand face up: this is the dummy. The declarer plays both their own cards and the dummy’s.

You must follow suit if you can. The highest card of the suit led wins the trick, unless someone plays a trump: then the highest trump wins. The winner leads the next trick.

When the app says “Play a card from the dummy”, tap a card in the dummy’s hand.

This is duplicate bridge: other players (bots) play the very same boards, so you are compared with them, not with luck. Your result is shown as matchpoints: the share of the field you beat. 50% is average.\n\nMaking your contract scores points. A game (3NT, 4♥, 4♠, 5♣ or 5♦ or more) and a slam (6 or 7) give big bonuses. If you win fewer tricks than you bid, the opponents score. A vulnerable side (Vul) gets bigger bonuses and bigger penalties.

A session is 16 boards. Your average matchpoints over the session is your result, and you can show it on the worldwide Top players list if you wish.

Board going badly? Undo takes back your last move, and Concede gives the rest of the tricks to the opponents.

Good luck, and enjoy the game!

Every deal starts with a round of bidding called the auction. The dealer speaks first, then each player in turn, clockwise.

On your turn you may:
• Bid: a level from 1 to 7 and a suit or NT (no trump), higher than the last bid. A bid of level N promises that your side will win N + 6 tricks (7 tricks for level 1, all 13 for level 7).
• Pass: say nothing.
• Double (X): say that the opponents' last bid is too high. In some positions it instead asks your partner to bid (see Takeout doubles).
• Redouble (XX): answer an opponent's double.

From lowest to highest the denominations go ♣ ♦ ♥ ♠ NT. So 1♠ is higher than 1♥, and 2♣ is higher than 1NT.

The auction ends when three players pass in a row after a bid. The last bid is the contract. The first player of the winning side who named that denomination becomes the declarer. The player on the declarer's left makes the opening lead, and the declarer's partner lays down the hand as the dummy.

Count high-card points (HCP): ace = 4, king = 3, queen = 2, jack = 1. The whole deck has 40, so an average hand has 10.

Shape matters too. A balanced hand has no void and no singleton: 4-3-3-3, 4-4-3-2 or 5-3-3-2. Any other hand is unbalanced, with a long or a short suit. Long suits take tricks, and a short suit helps when you play in a trump suit. The rules in this app mostly use points and suit lengths, as in the advice you see.

Combined strength of you and your partner:
• about 20 points: a part-score is possible
• 25 or more: game (3NT, 4♥, 4♠, 5♣ or 5♦)
• about 33 or more: a small slam (level 6)
• about 37 or more: a grand slam (level 7)

With your partner you try to find out three things:
1. How strong is the partnership: enough for game, or only a part-score?
2. Is there a trump suit? You want an eight-card fit: at least eight cards in one suit between the two of you. Hearts and spades score the game bonus at level 4, clubs and diamonds need level 5, and 3NT needs only level 3.
3. With no fit, play in no trump.

So look for a major-suit fit first, then no trump, then a minor suit.

Every bid is a message to your partner. You can only say your points and your suit lengths, so a bidding system is an agreed meaning for each bid. This app uses a simplified Standard American (SAYC-lite): five-card majors and a strong 1NT.

The first player to bid opens the auction. In this system:

• 1♣, 1♦, 1♥, 1♠: 12 to 21 points. A major (♥ or ♠) needs five cards; with five or more in both, bid the longer one (spades if they are equal). With no five-card major, open your longer minor: 1♦ with more diamonds than clubs (or equal with four or more), otherwise 1♣. A minor can be opened with only three cards.
• 1NT: 15 to 17 points, balanced (even with a five-card major).
• 2NT: 20 to 21 points, balanced.
• 2♣: 22 or more points. It is a very strong hand (see The strong 2♣ opening).
• Weak two (2♦, 2♥, 2♠): 5 to 11 points and a good six-card suit, with at least two of the three top honours. It blocks the opponents' bidding.
• Pre-empt at level 3: 5 to 10 points and a seven-card suit with at least 3 points in it.
• Pass: fewer than 12 points and no pre-empt.
Answering an opening of one in a suit

Your partner opened 1♣, 1♦, 1♥ or 1♠, which shows 12 to 21 points.

• 0 to 5 points: pass.
• 6 to 9 points: raise partner's major to level 2 with three or more cards; or show a four-card suit at the one level (your longest five-card suit, otherwise the cheapest four-card suit); or raise a minor to level 2 with five or more cards; or bid 1NT.
• 10 to 12 points: raise a major to level 3 (three or more cards) or a minor to level 3 (five or more), or show a new suit at level 2 (four or more cards in a minor, five or more in a major).
• 13 or more points: raise a major straight to game at level 4 (three or more cards). With a balanced hand and no suit to show, 2NT shows 13 to 15 points and 3NT shows 16 to 18.

Idea: raising partner's major shows support. A new suit looks for a better fit. 1NT is the answer with no fit and nothing better to say. When partner has opened a major, five cards plus your three make the eight-card fit.

1NT shows 15 to 17 points and a balanced hand. Your partner knows your strength at once and can decide.

The responder's choices:
• Pass: 0 to 7 points.
• 2NT: 8 or 9 points, an invitation. The opener bids 3NT with 16 or 17 points and passes with 15.
• 3NT: 10 to 17 points, game.
• 6NT: 18 or more points, a small slam.
• 2♣ (Stayman): 8 or more points and a four-card major. The opener answers 2♥ or 2♠ with a four-card major, and 2♦ with none.
• 2♦ (transfer): five or more hearts. The opener must bid 2♥. And 2♥ (transfer): five or more spades; the opener must bid 2♠. A transfer makes the strong hand the declarer, so its cards stay hidden.

After a transfer the responder bids again: 4 of the major with six cards and 10 or more points; 3NT with exactly five cards and 10 or more points; an invitation with 8 or 9 points (3 of the major with six cards, 2NT with five); pass with 0 to 7.

After you open one of a suit and your partner answers, you describe your hand again.

• Support partner's major with four cards: level 2 with 12 to 14 points, level 3 with 15 to 17, level 4 with 18 to 21.
• Show a new suit of four or more cards, at the one level or the two level.
• A balanced hand: 1NT with 12 to 14 points, 2NT with 18 to 19.
• Repeat your own suit when it has six cards (or five after a 1NT answer): level 2 with 12 to 15 points, level 3 with 16 to 21.
• A second suit that ranks higher than your first suit, bid at the two level (a reverse), needs 17 or more points.
• After a 1NT answer from your partner (6 to 12 points): pass with 12 to 17 points and nothing better to say, or 2NT with a balanced 18 or 19.

2♣ is the strongest opening: 22 or more points, a hand that may make game almost alone. It says nothing about clubs.

The responder:
• 2♦: waiting, with no good suit or fewer than 8 points.
• With 8 or more points and a good five-card suit (two of the top three honours): bid that suit (2♥, 2♠, 3♣ or 3♦). With 8 or more points and a balanced hand: 2NT.

The opener then continues: 2NT with 22 to 24 points balanced, 3NT with 25 to 27 balanced, or his own five-card suit (the longest). The partnership keeps bidding until game is reached.

The player on your right opens one of a suit and your partner has not bid yet:

• Suit overcall, with a five-card or longer suit: 8 to 16 points at the one level, or 11 to 16 points at the two level. The suit should have some strength (at least 3 points in it, or six cards).
• 1NT overcall: 15 to 18 balanced points, with a stopper in the opponents' suit (a card that stops them cashing the suit).
• Takeout double: 12 to 16 points, short in the opponents' suit and with support for the other suits (see Takeout doubles).
• Strong double: 17 or more points and short in their suit. You bid your own hand next.
• Pass: fewer than 8 points, or no suit.

When your partner overcalls and the next player passes, you advance:
• raise partner's suit with three-card support: 6 to 9 points one level up, 10 to 12 points two levels up, 13 or more points straight to game in a major;
• 1NT with 8 to 12 balanced points and a stopper;
• pass with 0 to 9 points.

A double of an opponent's opening bid of one in a suit, when your partner has not bid, is not a penalty double. It is a takeout double: it asks your partner to choose a suit.

To make one in this system you need 12 to 16 points, at most two cards in the opponents' suit and at least three cards in each other suit. (With 17 or more points you may double first and bid your own suit next.)

When your partner doubles, you must answer, even with no points:
• 0 to 8 points: bid your best suit (four or more cards, five-card suits first, majors preferred) at the cheapest level.
• 9 or more points: jump one level in that suit.
• 12 or more points and a four-card major: bid game at level 4.
• A balanced hand with a stopper in their suit: 1NT with 6 to 10 points, 3NT with 12 or more.
• With no four-card suit, bid your longest suit at the cheapest level.
When no rule fits: points and fit

In many positions the rule table gives no answer. Then the app works out the combined points: your points plus what your partner has shown so far. It chooses:
• 25 or more: game. 4♥ or 4♠ with an eight-card major fit (5♣ or 5♦ with a minor fit and 28 or more points), otherwise 3NT.
• 23 or 24: an invitation. 3 of the major with a major fit, or 2NT with a balanced hand and no fit.
• 19 or more, an eight-card fit, and the opponents are bidding: compete for the part-score at level 2 (level 3 with a nine-card fit).
• Otherwise: pass.

The app does not bid a slam in these positions, and it never goes past the level your combined strength supports.

• Prefer the major suits: hearts and spades count more towards game.
• When your partner has shown a range (for example 15 to 17 points), add your own points: you know at once how close game is.
• Do not bid again without a reason. After you have described your hand, let your partner decide.
• Vulnerability (Vul) raises both the bonuses and the penalties, so be more careful when you are vulnerable.
• Tap any call in the auction list to see what it means. The Advice button shows what the system would bid with your hand, and why.
• This is a simplified Standard American. Many conventions (for example Blackwood and Jacoby 2NT) are not included, so the bots bid slams only in a few simple cases, such as 6NT after a 1NT opening with 18 or more points.
